programme.desc: Carla Hall takes the lead in the kitchen as she introduces a playful and unexpected dish: fried Kool-Aid, inspired by nostalgic state fair treats from her childhood. Once tasted, both Clinton and Michael are pleasantly surprised, praising the light texture and more refined flavor compared to traditional fair versions. The episode transitions into a lively fan mail segment where the hosts debate their least favorite vegetables and share personal preferences, followed by a special “fan of the day” moment celebrating a crew member’s mother’s birthday with jokes and a spontaneous song from Clinton. The episode wraps with the hosts encouraging viewers to engage with the show and teasing future fun.

Michael demonstrates how to properly hold a chef’s knife, sharpen blades using a wheel sharpener, and explains the difference between honing and sharpening, while Clinton enthusiastically jumps in with detailed play-by-play commentary and cooking science facts. The hosts also passionately debate cutting boards, with Michael launching into a hilarious rant against plastic, ceramic, and glass boards in favor of traditional wood boards. Humor runs throughout the segment, including a conversation about Ginsu knives, microplastics, and Clinton’s grammar-school definition of “interjections.” The episode wraps with the “Fan of the Day” segment, where Lysa from Seattle wins a personalized video message from the hosts, followed by a final round of playful insults and banter before signing off.

The conversation centers around how technique can completely transform the same recipe, as Carla demonstrates both drop biscuits baked in muffin tins and laminated layered biscuits made through folding and stacking dough. Along the way, the hosts discuss the importance of cold butter, the role of steam in creating flaky layers, and why full-fat buttermilk makes a major difference in texture and tenderness. Michael and Clinton enthusiastically jump into the science behind baking while keeping the conversation playful, debating butter pockets, crispy edges, and the superiority of muffin-tin stuffing. Carla also shares clever practical tricks, including using oil instead of excess flour on the work surface and flipping biscuit dough for better height and rise. The trio reflects on how cooking competition shows continue to teach even experienced chefs new techniques, reinforcing the episode’s theme that cooking is a constant learning process. After pulling both styles of biscuits from the oven, the hosts compare the textures and flavors of each version while slathering them with butter, jam, and honey. The episode wraps with Carol from Columbus, Ohio being selected as the “Fan of the Day,” earning a personalized message from the hosts before everyone signs off stuffed and satisfied.

Woven into this history is the tale of two German brothers who were each involved with the secretive mission for the Third Reich. Ernst and Wernher von Braun were invited to come to the U.S. in Operation Paperclip, the secret United States intelligence program which employed German scientists after Germany surrendered. Both Ernst and von Braun were subsequently inaugurated in the International Space Hall of Fame as pioneers of the Space Age. For Friedrich, the outcome was very different. Nicolls has been sent by King Charles II to Reduce that people to an entire submission to us and secure that tradewhich the Dutch have wrongfully possessed themselves. He demands Stuyvesant and the town rendered to his majestys obedience, and protection. and has 96 cannons and three companies of troops to affect his orders. Stuyvesant, beset by decades of neglected defenses and the refusal of his own people to fight, surrenders without firing a shot. New Amsterdam becomes New Yorkfor nowas Charles provokes an all out war with the Dutch.

programme.title: Broadside
programme.desc: De Witt Meddles; God punishes London for Holmes Bonfire. Dutch are perhaps overconfident after the 4 Days Battle. But on Saint James Day they have fewer ships than the English (72 vs. 87) and, as usual, less firepower per ship. Moreover, unwisely, De Witt aligns his fleet to minimize the damage to certain flagships, which results in a cannon-duel favoring the English. De Witts meddling causes the Dutch to get much the worst of this battle. Blasting away for days in June and July, neither side can decisively follow up its victory. Tens of thousands killed, the wealth of both nations reduced to flotsam on the North Sea, and unspeakable hardships for each country...for what? Dutch privateers interdict coal bargesit will be very cold in London this winter. And, the Dutch are about to have a visit from Robert Holmes. Holmes gets a tip from a pusillanimous Dutchman about a large merchant fleet near the island of Terschelling. Holmes attacks, destroys one hundred fifty ships, and, to get his troops who are rampantly pillaging back on their ships, burns down Terschelling. Holmes Bonfire is a dangerous escalation of a horrific war. And, when the city of London burns to the ground a month later, many of the Dutch Elect see it as a work of God. Moreover, one Dutchman, Johan De Witt, plans to carry the war to the heart of England.
